rv.q: It is another extraordinary play from a writer seemingly capable of nothing else.

The gradual unfolding, with dialogue cushioned by considerable silences, becomes more and more absorbing, proving that when things drag in the theatre it is not because the pace is slow but because imaginative torpor has set in.
Infinite Life concludes with a remarkably moving moment of compassion and connection — a breakout from the isolating misery of pain.
Baker's weirdness and greatness are all her own.
James Macdonald directs, patiently and beautifully.
What multitudes Baker’s characters contain, even as they seem just to natter.

Baker's writing is frequently hilarious, taking relish in the absurdities of sphincters and fad diets and competitive suffering, making laughter catch your throat without ever surrendering to neat punchlines.
Baker’s plays are singular creations that march to their own rhythm, and we’re fortunate that four of them have now come to the National.
This is a terrific play, understated yet rich, utterly engrossing.
The close connection that Sofi and Eileen find in one another, bridging the vast generational gap, makes for a bittersweet final scene that brings this powerful play to a surprisingly positive close.
There is something deliciously understated in this production, and James Macdonald's direction allows moments to linger and sink in.
Infinite Life doesn’t feel like a play but a prank staged by psychologists who want to see how much vacuous poppycock a paying audience will bear before they demand a refund.

cn.t: Baker's slow-burn meditation on chronic pain and female friendship at a California fasting clinic earns widespread acclaim for its humane observation, dark humor, and exquisite performances, though its glacial pacing proves divisive.
